issues.description: The manuscript gives irreconcilable descriptions of the sample. The abstract and introduction frame the study as a five-year analysis in a national probability/general population sample, but the Methods state that participants were recruited from an introductory psychology participant pool and were mostly 19-year-old students. This makes the actual data source unclear and calls into question all inferential claims, including the title, abstract, and general-population framing.
issues.quote: We examine the longitudinal influence of SDO and RWA on people’s willingness to change their behaviour to benefit the environment in a national probability sample over five years. / We recruited participants through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington. / Of the 374 participants included in this study, the average age was 19 years at Time 1 (2009; M = 19.42, SD = 2.31) and 68% were female.

issues.description: The paper repeatedly claims national representativeness and high generalizability, but the described sample is a narrow student sample. This is not a minor wording issue: it invalidates the external-validity claims and substantially overstates the scope of the findings.
issues.quote: Our research uses a nationally representative sample, meaning that our results are highly generalisable, at least to the New Zealand population. / Using a nationally representative sample, we tested the strength of associations between SDO, RWA, and environmentalism over time.

issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly refers to the NZAVS website, technical documents, and team acknowledgments, despite the Methods describing a university participant-pool sample. This suggests the manuscript may conflate two different datasets or studies. Readers cannot determine what dataset was analyzed, making the work difficult to verify or replicate.
issues.quote: Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website. / We express our gratitude to the New Zealand Attitudes and Values Study (NZAVS) team for their work collecting and maintaining the NZAVS.

issues.description: The central dependent variable is described as willingness to change behavior or make sacrifices for the environment, but the Methods define it using two items about environmental concern and perceived exaggeration of environmental problems. These are not equivalent constructs. A concern/skepticism measure cannot straightforwardly support conclusions about willingness to sacrifice or behavioral change.
issues.quote: We examine the longitudinal influence of SDO and RWA on people’s willingness to change their behaviour to benefit the environment... / Environmentalism was measured as participants’ concern about environmental problems. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley’s [28] environmental concern scale, "How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?" and "To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?"

issues.description: Even apart from the mislabeling, the environmental outcome is measured with only two items that capture concern and skepticism rather than the broader construct of environmentalism. This narrow operationalization limits content validity and makes the broad claims about environmentalism overly strong.
issues.quote: Environmentalism was measured as participants’ concern about environmental problems. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley’s [28] environmental concern scale, "How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?" and "To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?"

issues.description: One RWA item was omitted at Time 2, meaning the construct is not measured identically across all waves. This threatens longitudinal comparability, especially when the analysis assumes stationarity and compares paths across time. The manuscript does not explain how this non-equivalence was handled.
issues.quote: The item "Some of the best people in our country are those who are challenging our government, criticizing religion, and ignoring the “normal way” things are supposed to be done", was not assessed at time two, but included in all other time points.

issues.description: For longitudinal models involving latent constructs or repeated composite measures, it is important to establish that the same construct is being measured in the same way over time. The manuscript mentions equality constraints on residual variances, but does not report any tests of configural, metric, or scalar invariance. Without this, apparent change or cross-lagged effects may reflect measurement changes rather than substantive change.
issues.quote: We tested the reciprocal influences between the constructs with a stationary cross-lagged model where all parameters are set as time-invariant. ... We also constrained to equality the residual variance for the same item over time, so item 1 in the SDO scale had equal residual variance across all time points.

issues.description: Using listwise deletion in a five-wave longitudinal study can introduce bias unless data are missing completely at random, and it wastes information in the presence of attrition. No justification, missingness analysis, or sensitivity analysis is provided. This is particularly problematic given the omitted RWA item at Time 2 and likely longitudinal dropout.
issues.quote: Analyses were conducted using listwise deletion.

issues.description: Attrition and retention are central to interpreting longitudinal findings, especially when listwise deletion is used. The manuscript does not report per-wave sample sizes, retention rates, or whether attrition was selective, instead directing readers elsewhere. This prevents evaluation of attrition bias.
issues.quote: Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website.

issues.description: The analytic model is not described with enough detail to reproduce or evaluate it. It is unclear whether the analysis used observed scale scores or latent variables, which estimator was used, how Likert items were treated, how reverse-coded items were scored, how cross-sectional residual covariances were handled, and how the missing RWA item at Time 2 was incorporated. Deferring syntax until acceptance is not sufficient for review.
issues.quote: We used path analysis to examine associations between SDO, RWA and willingness to sacrifice for the environment. The model included three variables across five measurement points and was conducted in Mplus (version 7.3 [29]). A copy of the Mplus syntax used will be available on the NZAVS website upon acceptance of the manuscript.

issues.description: The model imposes equality constraints across all waves, assuming the same autoregressive and cross-lagged dynamics at every interval. This is a strong assumption that should be tested rather than imposed because the authors are interested in overall effects. If the true effects vary across time, the constrained model can yield misleading estimates.
issues.quote: We tested the reciprocal influences between the constructs with a stationary cross-lagged model where all parameters are set as time-invariant. ... We imposed this stationary cross-lagged model because we were more interested in the overall and comparative effects of SDO and RWA on changes in environmentalism, and not on whether these effects change during the interval measured.

issues.description: The timing of measurement occasions is inconsistent and unclear. The paper is framed as a five-year analysis, but the Methods say participants took part across five semesters from 2009 to 2013. Cross-lagged coefficients depend on interval length, so ambiguity about spacing undermines interpretation.
issues.quote: This study uses data from individuals who participated across five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013). / Full title: The influence of social dominance orientation and right-wing authoritarianism on environmentalism: A five-year cross-lagged analysis

issues.description: The model shows poor fit on a key incremental fit index (CFI = .86), yet is accepted largely because RMSEA and SRMR are better. Dismissing poor CFI as being 'affected by model complexity' is not enough, especially for a model used to make directional and causal claims. The low CFI suggests meaningful misspecification.
issues.quote: Overall, model fit was poorer for those indices affected by model complexity (e.g. χ2(2279) = 36511.73, p < .001, CFI = .86), however those less influenced by complexity pointed to good fit (RMSEA = .03, 90% CI [.025, .026], SRMR = .07), therefore the model was accepted.

issues.description: The authors tested whether the SDO→environmentalism and RWA→environmentalism paths differ, found a non-significant difference test, and then still concluded that SDO is the stronger predictor based on the raw coefficients. That is not a valid statistical inference. If the equality constraint does not worsen fit, there is no statistical support for claiming the two paths differ.
issues.quote: We found that our original model provides comparable fit to the data 2(1) = 2.34, p = .126, but based on the pattern of unstandardized coefficients we interpret SDO as a stronger predictor of change in willingness to sacrifice for the environment than RWA in our sample.

issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly treats cross-lagged associations as evidence of causal pathways and directionality. Standard cross-lagged panel models on observational data do not establish causality and are known to confound stable between-person differences with within-person dynamics. Without stronger designs or models, the causal wording is not justified.
issues.quote: These analyses help us disentangle the directionality of the relationships... / These results suggest that there is a causal pathway from ideological attitudes to environmentalism.

issues.description: The conclusions go beyond the data by inferring the specific motivations underlying the associations. The study measures ideological attitudes and an environmental attitude variable; it does not measure 'motivation to exploit the environment,' 'desire for dominance over nature,' or 'desire to submit to tradition and authority.' These mechanistic claims are speculative.
issues.quote: These findings suggest that the motivation to exploit the environment comes primarily from the desire for dominance, and to a lesser extent from the desire to submit to tradition and authority.

issues.description: The model includes only three variables. No demographic, political, socioeconomic, or personality covariates are modeled, despite their plausible relationships with both ideological attitudes and environmentalism. The resulting cross-lagged paths may reflect confounding rather than specific effects of SDO or RWA.
issues.quote: The model included three variables across five measurement points

issues.description: The manuscript gives inconsistent significance thresholds and a confused justification. The Methods state p < .05 because of the 'large sample size,' while the figure caption says the accepted threshold is p < .01. This inconsistency makes it unclear what inferential standard was actually used.
issues.quote: Because of the large sample size of this dataset, we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings. / Figure 1. Unstandardized parameters assessing the association between SDO, RWA, and willingness to sacrifice for the environment (WILL). All meet our accepted threshold for significance of p < .01 unless otherwise noted.

issues.description: The manuscript states that standardized parameters are presented, but the figure caption says the parameters are unstandardized. Because claims about comparative strength hinge on coefficient size, this inconsistency materially affects interpretation.
issues.quote: We present standardized parameters, which vary across time points due to differences in observed variances. / Figure 1. Unstandardized parameters assessing the association between SDO, RWA, and willingness to sacrifice for the environment (WILL).

issues.description: The paper claims that one correlation is stronger than another because their confidence intervals do not overlap. That is not the correct method for comparing two dependent correlations that share a variable. A formal test for dependent correlations is required.
issues.quote: Of note here is that the zero-order correlation between SDO and environmentalism was stronger than the correlation for RWA, as indicated by the non-overlapping confidence interval.

issues.description: The reported chi-square difference statistic is extraordinarily large for a 1-df comparison of two lagged effects and is not explained. Combined with the malformed notation ('2(1)' instead of χ²(1)), this raises concerns about reporting accuracy or analytic errors.
issues.quote: These lagged effects were also statistically different (2(1) = 15,389.13, p < .001)

issues.description: The paper infers a broad societal socialization process from a single asymmetry in cross-lagged paths. Even if the asymmetry were estimated correctly, it would not justify claims about how 'New Zealanders' are socialized. Such an inference requires comparative or contextual evidence beyond this model.
issues.quote: Because we found that RWA predicts SDO over time, but SDO does not predict RWA, this suggests that New Zealander’s are socialized into authoritarianism to a greater extent than social dominance.

issues.description: The described sample is demographically narrow: very young, majority female, and overwhelmingly Pākehā. Even if the recruitment-source contradiction were ignored, this composition is not representative of the general population, so claims about the broader New Zealand public are not supported.
issues.quote: Of the 374 participants included in this study, the average age was 19 years at Time 1 (2009; M = 19.42, SD = 2.31) and 68% were female. Furthermore, 76% of participants were born in New Zealand and the majority (86%) identified as Pākehā (New Zealand European).

issues.description: The same outcome is labeled throughout the manuscript as environmentalism, concern about environmental problems, willingness to make sacrifices, willingness to sacrifice, and willingness to change behavior. These are distinct constructs. The inconsistent terminology obscures what was actually measured and analyzed.
issues.quote: Environmentalism was measured as participants’ concern about environmental problems. / SDO = social dominance orientation, RWA = right-wing authoritarianism, WILL = willingness to make sacrifices for the environment. / We used path analysis to examine associations between SDO, RWA and willingness to sacrifice for the environment.

issues.description: The model description appears internally inconsistent and incomplete: the manuscript says all parameters were set time-invariant, then repeats the same statement about constraining cross-lagged paths twice, without clearly describing which other parameters were constrained or how latent variables were specified. This hampers reproducibility and raises concern about analytic documentation quality.
issues.quote: We tested the reciprocal influences between the constructs with a stationary cross-lagged model where all parameters are set as time-invariant. We started by constraining the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point. ... Finally, we constrained the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point.

issues.description: The path coefficients report 'SD' alongside B values, but in this context the uncertainty term should be a standard error, not a standard deviation. This is a technical reporting error that creates ambiguity about what quantity is being presented.
issues.quote: SDO was a stronger predictor of change in environmental sacrifice (B = -.11, SD = .01, p < .001, 95% CI [-.13, -.09]) than RWA (B = -.02, SD = .01, p = .001, 95% CI [-.05, -.01]).
